title: Does hot water freeze faster than cold?
hook: A schoolboy in Tanzania thought so. Physicists still argue about it.
summary: It is sometimes reported, but disputed: results depend on conditions and even on how the effect is defined.

cardBlocks.text: In the 1960s, a Tanzanian student, Erasto Mpemba, noticed that a hot ice cream mix froze before a cold one. He studied it with the physicist Denis Osborne, and the idea that very hot liquids can freeze faster than colder ones became known as the Mpemba effect.

The effect is disputed, though. It doesn’t show up in every setting or experiment, and studies with water have mixed results: some found nothing reproducible. Physicists don’t even agree on its definition. In a 2016 study, researchers cooled water under carefully controlled conditions and concluded there was no evidence for meaningful observations of the effect.
The Mpemba effect is disputed: hot water has been reported to freeze first, but controlled experiments don’t always agree.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Part of the argument is about definitions. "Freezing" can mean the moment a surface layer of ice appears or the moment the liquid is completely solid, which makes experiments hard to compare.
References to the idea that hot water cools faster go back to Aristotle. In 2012, the UK’s Royal Society of Chemistry even ran a competition for explanations of the effect.
